blocks.cap: A number you know, ringing out into the dark

blocks.p: The call log had become a column of his brother's name. Gin, Gin, Gin, all the way down the screen in small red letters, like names cut into a memorial stone.

Rei sat at the kitchen table under the one lamp and looked at it. Outside, the cicadas had not stopped since noon. Somewhere along the canal a neighbour was hanging the first Obon lantern of the week, and the paper box knocked against its pole in the warm wind with a sound like a knuckle on a door.

He had called nineteen times since the hook by the door came up empty. Each time the line had rung on and on into a silence that did not feel empty. It felt held. It was the silence of a phone lying in someone's hand while that someone decided whether to answer it.

He told himself it was only a dead battery. A phone in a drawer. Gin forgot things. Gin had once left his phone in a bowl of rice for two days because he had been drying it and then forgotten it was there. Rei held on to that story for as long as it would hold him.
Then he pressed the name a twentieth time.
It rang twice. Then the ringing stopped, and there was no voicemail tone, no hiss of a pocket, nothing. Only breathing. It was slow and level and a little too careful, like someone counting.
"Rei."

It was Gin's voice. Every part of it was right, the slight roughness at the bottom, the way the name tilted up at the end. It was right the way a photograph is right. Nothing moved behind it. It said his name as if it were reading the word off a card it had been handed.
Rei's mouth had gone dry. He had planned a dozen things to say and every one of them fell away. What came out was the oldest thing he had.
"Gin. Nii-san. It's me. Talk to me."
Something on the other end caught. It was not a word. It was a breath taken wrong, the way a man breathes when he has been held under water and his face has just broken the surface.
"Go home." The voice was suddenly ragged, frightened, close to the phone. It was Gin, all of him, for the length of one sentence. "This isn't a thing you walk toward and walk back from the same."
Then it was gone. Rei heard it go. The breath smoothed out. The silence came back over the line like water closing over a dropped stone.
"Gin?"
"I'm here." Calm again. Courteous. "I'm sorry. I'm very tired, Rei. I didn't mean to frighten you."

Rei pressed the phone so hard against his ear that it hurt. He had heard that broken breath before. He had heard it every time Gin came up out of a bad dream in the next room, years ago, and called out to check that Rei was still there.

And he knew, from somewhere, how long it had lasted. He had read it once in Gin's book, in a chapter about reading the possessed from the outside, and had pushed the page away because it was about strangers. One line had stuck to him anyway. Brief surface moments, four seconds, sometimes less, where the original person's emotional register breaks through before being suppressed again.
Less time than it took to say a sentence. That was what his brother had been able to steal back.

blocks.cap: The two voices, learning to rhyme

blocks.p: The smooth voice did not hang up. That frightened him more than anything it said.

It talked to him instead, gently, the way Gin used to talk him down at three in the morning when exams were close and the walls felt near. It asked if he had eaten. It asked if he was sleeping. And then, without ever seeming to change the subject, it began to explain.

"Do you remember the spring of 2011?" it said. "You were fifteen. You watched the water on the television for a week and stopped eating. I remember." A pause, perfectly timed. "Twenty thousand people, Rei. Most of them were never given their rites. No grave, no name read out, nobody to set them down. They are still waiting. The membrane over Kita has been weeping for them ever since. You've felt it. Don't tell me you haven't."
Rei said nothing. He had felt it. He had felt it walking to the konbini at night, a heaviness in the air near the river that he had always put down to the humidity.

"Something is owed to them," the voice said. "Someone with the right grade, and the right grief, could finally close that wound. What looks like a catastrophe to a frightened intern looks different from higher up. From there it looks like a debt being paid at last."

It was not lying. That was the horror of it. Every piece was true. The dead were real and the weeping was real and the debt, Rei thought, might even be real. The voice simply stacked the true things at an angle, one on another, until the angle pointed somewhere he could not see.
And he found himself nodding in the empty kitchen.

He stopped. He put his free hand flat on the table and felt the wood, the old knife scar near the edge where Gin had once cut bread without a board. He made himself listen again, not to the words, but to what the words wanted.
The broken voice had wanted one thing. Go home. It wanted him away, safe, out of it. It asked nothing for itself.
The smooth voice wanted him closer.
"I could use your help," it was saying now, softly. "Not tonight. Soon. There are things I can't carry alone anymore. You were always good at noticing what other people miss."

A thing that means to close a wound needs hands. Rei understood that, sitting there under the lamp. It needed hands it could call its own, and a brother's love was the strongest leash anyone had ever been offered.
"Where are you?" he asked.
The voice laughed, very kindly. "Get some sleep, Rei." And the line went dead.
He sat for a long time with the phone in his lap. The lantern outside knocked against its pole. Gin's coat still hung on the back of the other chair, where it had hung since May.
At ten past two the phone buzzed once. A voicemail. No call had come through. He played it with his thumb shaking.
The voice on it was so faint it was almost only breath, and it was almost Gin. It said six words, fast, as if someone might take the phone away before the last one.
"Third drawer. Under the charger. Read."
